name: First Great Awakening
also_known_as: The Great Awakening; the Evangelical Revival (in Britain)
summary: A wave of revivals in the British American colonies, linked to the Evangelical Revival in Britain, which stressed personal conversion, divided churches into supporters and opponents, and shaped American evangelicalism.

start.label: Revival begins in Jonathan Edwards's Northampton church

end.label: Revival fades amid division between New Lights and Old Lights

key_dates.label: George Whitefield begins his great American preaching tour
Gilbert Tennent preaches 'The Danger of an Unconverted Ministry'
Edwards preaches 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God'; Presbyterian Old Side–New Side split
Connecticut passes a law against itinerant preachers
James Davenport's book-burning at New London; Charles Chauncy's Seasonable Thoughts attacks the revival

background.text: Earlier local revivals had occurred under Theodorus Frelinghuysen in New Jersey (1720s) and Solomon Stoddard in Northampton; Presbyterians trained at William Tennent's 'Log College' in Pennsylvania spread revival preaching.

happened.text: Jonathan Edwards's Northampton revival (1734–35), described in his Faithful Narrative, became a model for revival across the colonies and in Britain.
George Whitefield's tours from 1739 drew crowds of thousands, sometimes tens of thousands, from Georgia to New England, and spread the revival across denominational lines.
Preachers stressed the 'new birth', a felt experience of conversion; some meetings saw crying out, fainting, and visions, which critics called 'enthusiasm'.

Churches split between 'New Lights' (supporters) and 'Old Lights' (opponents): Presbyterians divided into Old Side and New Side synods (1741–58), and many New England congregations broke away as 'Separates', some becoming Baptists.
The revival reached enslaved Africans and Native Americans, some of whom, like the Mohegan minister Samson Occom, became preachers.

participants.name: Jonathan Edwards
participants.role: Leading preacher and theologian of the revival

participants.name: George Whitefield
participants.role: Itinerant evangelist whose tours spread the revival

participants.name: John Wesley
participants.role: Leader of the parallel Evangelical Revival in Britain

participants.name: Charles Wesley
participants.role: Hymn writer of the Evangelical Revival in Britain

participants.name: Charles Chauncy
participants.role: Boston minister and leading critic of the revival

outcomes.text: It shaped the evangelical emphasis on conversion and helped Baptists and later Methodists grow in America.
Revivalists founded colleges to train ministers, including the College of New Jersey (Princeton, 1746), Brown (1764), and Dartmouth (1769).
Some historians argue it weakened established churches and prepared the ground for religious liberty and the American Revolution; others question how unified a movement it was.

condemnations_note: The revival divided churches but led to few formal condemnations of individuals; the courts that judged James Davenport found him mentally disturbed rather than guilty.

condemnations.reason: The revivalist New Brunswick Presbytery excluded from the synod

persecution_note: Opponents used colonial law against radical revivalists, and Separates and Baptists were taxed and punished for refusing to support established churches.

persecution.title: Connecticut's law against itinerant preaching
persecution.summary: Connecticut's assembly passed a law allowing itinerant preachers to be expelled and ministers who preached in other parishes without permission to lose their salaries. Separates who refused to pay taxes for the established Congregational churches were fined or jailed.
persecution.outcome: Repealed in 1750; Separates and Baptists campaigned for religious liberty.

persecution.title: Arrest and deportation of James Davenport
persecution.summary: The radical itinerant James Davenport, who denounced ministers as unconverted, was arrested in Connecticut and deported, and later tried in Boston; both courts judged him mentally disturbed. In 1743 he led a bonfire of books and luxury goods at New London, which he later repented.
persecution.outcome: Deported; he retracted his excesses in 1744.
